analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers for their carbon emissions and sends the money back to workers, retirees, and states.
analysis.headline: The Senate's carbon fee bill, introduced by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse with one cosponsor, never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill puts a fee on coal, oil, and natural gas based on the carbon dioxide released when they burn, starting at $49 per ton in 2018 and rising 2% a year plus inflation until U.S. emissions fall to 20% of 2005 levels [S3]. It also charges for methane leaks and other greenhouse gases across the fuel supply chain, and for fluorinated gases [S2]. The money comes back to people through a refundable tax credit of up to $550 per worker ($1,100 for couples), annual payments to Social Security, veterans, and disability beneficiaries, and $10 billion a year in state grants for low-income and rural households plus retraining for fossil fuel workers [S3]. It also cuts the corporate income tax rate from 35% to 29% [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Working people get a refundable credit worth up to $550 a year per worker; retirees, veterans, and disabled Americans get an equal annual payment; low-income and rural households get state-administered rebates to cover higher energy bills; fossil fuel workers get priority for job training and transition assistance [S3]. Corporations get a lower tax rate [S3]. Studies of carbon fee-and-dividend designs generally find the rebates outweigh the higher energy costs for most low- and middle-income households.

how_it_helps.text: Workers earning income get a fully refundable credit equal to the lesser of 6.2% of earned income or $550 per year, doubled to $1,100 on joint returns, and the credit cannot be counted against them in other benefit programs [S3].
Social Security beneficiaries, veterans, and disabled Americans — who don't file tax returns — receive an equal annual payment disbursed between April 1 and May 15 [S3].

States share $10 billion a year (rising with inflation) to rebate higher energy costs to households below 150% of the poverty line, help rural households, and provide job training with priority for fossil fuel workers [S3].
The fee is designed to make clean energy relatively cheaper without a hard regulatory mandate, and rises automatically until national emissions fall to 20% of 2005 levels [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers pay the fee at the mine, refinery, or processor, and the bill adds a supplement after 2020 to cover methane leaks and flaring across their supply chains [S3]. Energy prices for consumers rise; the credits and rebates are meant to offset that for most households. Corporations benefit from the rate cut but the fee revenue that funds it is money not available for larger rebates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The fee starts at $49 per ton of carbon dioxide, which would raise gasoline, heating, and electricity prices immediately, while the offsetting credits and rebates arrive on a different schedule — leaving households temporarily out of pocket [S3].
Cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 29% returns a large share of the fee revenue to company shareholders rather than to households, weakening how progressive the bill is overall [S3].
The burden falls unevenly by region and lifestyle: households in coal-dependent states or with long commutes pay more in energy costs than the flat $550 credit offsets [S3].
$49 per ton is well below what many economists estimate is needed to fully price climate damage, so the bill is a floor, not a complete fix [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is serious: the fee rises automatically until emissions drop 80% below 2005 levels, supply-chain methane leaks are charged too, and border adjustments protect manufacturers from losing out to countries without carbon fees [S3]. The main honest criticisms are the corporate rate cut, which diverts revenue away from households, and the gap between when energy prices rise and when rebates arrive. On net, most working households come out ahead, and the chief costs fall on fossil fuel producers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), joined by Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI), introduced the bill on July 26, 2017 [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the record for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers continued emitting without paying any carbon fee, and no national carbon pricing advanced. Energy-intensive manufacturers avoided any new cost as well. Ordinary people got neither the higher energy prices nor the rebates — the status quo held.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led Finance Committee and Senate majority took no action on it [S3, S4, S5].

industries.note: Coal would pay the full $49-per-ton fee at the mine, rising yearly, plus a supplement after 2020 covering methane emissions from mining. Coal is the most carbon-intensive fuel, so the fee hits it hardest — the industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the public's interest in cutting emissions.

Petroleum and natural gas are charged at the refinery and processor level, and after 2020 the fee is raised to cover methane from leaks, venting, and flaring across the supply chain — a direct cost the industry has historically avoided pricing.

industries.industry: Fossil-fuel power plants and other large emitters
industries.note: Facilities emitting over 25,000 tons a year pay fees on non-fuel greenhouse gas emissions, and fluorinated gas makers and users face a fee phased in through 2029.

The bill charges them on energy inputs but refunds the cost on exports, charges an equivalent fee on competing imports, and recognizes foreign carbon policies — designed so they don't lose to unregulated competitors. Their interest in these protections runs alongside keeping the climate policy effective.

The bill cuts the corporate income rate from 35% to 29% on income over $75,000, funded from carbon fee revenue — a benefit to shareholders paid for with revenue that could otherwise enlarge household rebates.
